29:45.en: Recite that which hath been inspired in thee of the Scripture, and establish worship. Lo! worship preserveth from lewdness and iniquity, but verily remembrance of Allah is more important. And Allah knoweth what ye do

do0on_YAhRk.title: Ramadan 2023, Night 23: Tahajjud
do0on_YAhRk.one_line: Between rakaat: a walk through the meanings of the prayer from standing to taslim, then a warning about arrogance, showing off and envy.
do0on_YAhRk.summary: Night twenty-three carries two reminders between sets of rakaat. In the first, the sheikh continues his walk through the prayer itself, starting from the verse that prayer restrains a person from indecency and wrongdoing. He moves through its stations in order: the bowing with its glorification of the Lord the Magnificent, the prostrations and the short dua between them asking Allah for mercy, well-being and guidance, then the tashahhud with its greetings to Allah, its salam on the Prophet and on the righteous servants, the testimony of faith and the salawat, and finally the closing salam. Along the way he brings in the hadith that real patience shows at the first blow. The point is that the words people repeat in every prayer should carry meaning for them in the rakaat they are about to pray. The second reminder turns to the hidden diseases of the heart that damage a person's relationship with Allah: self-admiration, arrogance, showing off and envy. He prescribes frequent istighfar as the remedy, then returns to envy with examples from how people deal with one another.

hadith.gist: Patience is truly shown at the first blow of a calamity.
The dua between the two prostrations: O Allah forgive me, have mercy on me, grant me well-being and guide me.
The wording of the tashahhud the Prophet taught: greetings, prayers and good things are for Allah, peace on the Prophet and on Allah's righteous servants.

takeaways: Judge your prayer by whether it keeps you away from indecency and wrongdoing.
Know and mean the words of each position: the glorification in ruku, the dua between the prostrations, the tashahhud.

35:28.ar: وَمِنَ ٱلنَّاسِ وَٱلدَّوَآبِّ وَٱلۡأَنۡعَٰمِ مُخۡتَلِفٌ أَلۡوَٰنُهُۥ كَذَٰلِكَۗ إِنَّمَا يَخۡشَى ٱللَّهَ مِنۡ عِبَادِهِ ٱلۡعُلَمَٰٓؤُاْۗ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَزِيزٌ غَفُورٌ

4:1.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّاسُ ٱتَّقُواْ رَبَّكُمُ ٱلَّذِي خَلَقَكُم مِّن نَّفۡسࣲ وَٰحِدَةࣲ وَخَلَقَ مِنۡهَا زَوۡجَهَا وَبَثَّ مِنۡهُمَا رِجَالࣰ ا كَثِيرࣰ ا وَنِسَآءࣰۚ وَٱتَّقُواْ ٱللَّهَ ٱلَّذِي تَسَآءَلُونَ بِهِۦ وَٱلۡأَرۡحَامَۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ كَانَ عَلَيۡكُمۡ رَقِيبࣰ ا
4:1.en: O mankind! Be careful of your duty to your Lord Who created you from a single soul and from it created its mate and from them twain hath spread abroad a multitude of men and women. We are weary of one kind of food; so call upon thy Lord for us that He bring forth for us of that which the earth groweth - of its herbs and its cucumbers and its corn and its lentils and its onions. He said: Would ye exchange that which is higher for that which is lower? Go down to settled country, thus ye shall get that which ye demand. k6JfvO-4K48.speaker_note: Third session of his own Facing Disbelief series at his masjid; refers to his cancer practice
k6JfvO-4K48.title: Facing Disbelief 3: Life as the Second Source, and an Approach to Evolution
k6JfvO-4K48.one_line: Fine-tuning of life as evidence of a cause, and why evolution, read alongside the Quran on gradual creation and Adam, poses no threat to faith.
k6JfvO-4K48.summary: He defines eman as following the view with uniform evidence that lacks proof the senses can touch, rejecting Dawkins's definition of faith as belief against evidence. He then surveys the fine-tuning of life: Earth's distance from the sun, the moon's size and tilt, the magnetic field, water, carbon, tectonic plates, oxygen, and the odds of one in 700 quintillion, so the real question is luck or cause. Scientists like Einstein and Darwin rejected the scriptural God of anthropomorphism, not a power behind creation, and the Quran says scholars revere Allah because understanding the how deepens awe. He outlines evolution's core claims and insists there is no Islamic reason to fight a scientific theory: it explains Allah's tools, not His absence, and Dawkins's god-of-the-gaps argument attacks a straw man. The Quran describes gradual creation; be and it is carries no word for immediately, and six days means six periods. On Adam, he reads the teaching of names, the choosing of Adam among others, and the comparison with Isa as compatible with a cognitive leap in an existing lineage, and treats hadith on Adam's creation as metaphorical. He argues Adam's garden was on earth, and ends with what science cannot explain: being from nothing, life from death, and life's drive to live.

outline.heading: Opening
Defining eman
outline.gist: Faith is following the opinion with uniform evidence that lacks sense-based proof, not believing blindly against all evidence as Dawkins defines it.

outline.heading: Why the unseen is hard for us
outline.gist: The Quran forbids belief against evidence; humans engage the world through the senses, which is why belief without sensory contact feels incomplete.

outline.heading: Evidence is stronger than physical proof
outline.gist: If a Muslim does not see uniform evidence for Allah something is missing; uniform evidence outweighs scientific proof.

outline.heading: Fine-tuning: the sun and the moon
outline.gist: Earth sits at exactly the right distance from the sun, and the moon's size and distance create the tilt, seasons and tides life needed to leave the sea.

outline.heading: Fine-tuning: size, magnetic field, water and carbon
outline.gist: Earth's gravity, its magnetic shield against solar rays, its proportion of water and the stability of carbon all had to be just right.

outline.heading: Fine-tuning: tectonic plates, oxygen and the first cells
outline.gist: Plate movement released gases at the right rate, oxygen is held at a level that does not burn everything, and early organisms released oxygen rather than dying out.

outline.heading: One in 700 quintillion
outline.gist: Scientists put the chance of life arising at astronomically low odds; Martin Rees's Just Six Numbers leads some to glorify Allah and others to disbelieve.

outline.heading: Six numbers: luck or cause?
outline.gist: Fundamental constants that science measures but never explains; the question becomes whether existence is luck or caused.

outline.heading: Einstein, Darwin and Spinoza's God
outline.gist: Both rejected the humanised God of the church, not a power behind existence; Einstein's Spinozan God resembles the pantheism some Sufis proposed, which Islamic creed rejects.

outline.heading: Those who revere Allah are the scholars
outline.gist: The verse says scholars revere Allah, not that they believe; science offers the how, never the who or why, so belief must come first.

outline.heading: Understanding the how deepens awe
outline.gist: Grasping a single cell pathway is overwhelming; an evidence-based mind would not accept luck as the explanation.

outline.heading: The lottery won thirty days running
outline.gist: The odds of chance life equal one person winning a lottery among eight billion every day for a month.

outline.heading: The five claims of evolution
outline.gist: Reproduction of like kind, survival, mutation, natural selection and survival of the fittest.

outline.heading: No Islamic reason to fight a scientific theory
outline.gist: He is indifferent to evolution itself, and surveys rank it lowest among causes of doubt, but combating science reflects a misunderstanding of faith.

outline.heading: Evolution says nothing about God's existence
outline.gist: It explains how life came about; Dawkins's skill was using it to attack religion.

outline.heading: The god of the gaps as a straw man
outline.gist: Muslims never used Allah to fill gaps in knowledge but see Him as the driving cause, with science revealing His tools, though some religious people do think in gaps.

outline.heading: The Quran on gradual creation
outline.gist: Creation from one soul and every creature from water, some on bellies, some on two legs or four: life appearing in stages, not all at once.

outline.heading: The 'Mohammedan theory'
outline.gist: Opponents of Darwin called it a Muslim idea, since Muslim scholars had long discussed gradual development drawn from the Quran.

outline.heading: Be and it is, and six days
outline.gist: If creation were instant, six days would make no sense; the word immediately is assumed by the reader, not stated in the verse.

outline.heading: Borrowed images of God
outline.gist: Muslims absorbed medieval and minority-era images of God zapping things into being; the series aims to know Allah as the Quran presents Him.

outline.heading: Young-earth claims are not Quranic
outline.gist: Biblical chronology fixes the earth at six thousand years, which Dawkins exploited; the Quran's thousand and fifty thousand are Arab idioms for vast spans.

outline.heading: The chef and the oven
outline.gist: Saying evolution made life is like saying the oven made the meal; a tool does not deny the cook.

outline.heading: Travel and see how He began creation
outline.gist: Allah invites people to research how life began, which He would not ask if it were impossible to find.

outline.heading: Microevolution and macroevolution as tools
outline.gist: The peppered moth shows observable change; randomness and mutation are tools Allah used and do not deny a cause.

outline.heading: Figuring out the trick
outline.gist: Explaining a trick only discredits a performer who claimed it could never be explained, and Allah said the opposite: learn and you will see.

outline.heading: Six days as six periods
outline.gist: Six and seven in Arabic signify length and endless repetition; a day means a period of time, perhaps the seasons with night and day.

outline.heading: The real difficulty: Adam
outline.gist: Muslims accept evolution for other creatures; the struggle is Adam, who is a real individual and the first human, though perhaps not the first Homo sapiens.

outline.heading: A sudden cognitive leap
outline.gist: Evolutionary science points to an abrupt jump in metacognition and language rather than gradual change.

outline.heading: He taught Adam the names
outline.gist: What made Adam unique was articulation: naming and describing abstract ideas, not laws or ethics.

outline.heading: Adam chosen like Nuh and the family of Ibrahim
outline.gist: Choosing implies selection from among similar beings, as with the others listed in the same verse.

outline.heading: Raised from the descendants of other people
outline.gist: Allah could replace humanity as He produced it from the offspring of another people; nothing limits this to Quraysh.

outline.heading: The Quran is not a biology book
outline.gist: Its wording stays open to science; it explains who we are, why we are here and who put us here, while science supplies the how.

outline.heading: Isa is like Adam
outline.gist: Isa was carried in a womb yet called created from dust; the likeness is that both involve something unclear to us, so the verse supports rather than refutes this view.

outline.heading: From clay to the breathing of the spirit
outline.gist: Creation began from clay, then descendants from fluid, then proportion and Allah's spirit, which is beyond science.

outline.heading: Created with My two hands
outline.gist: Metaphor blindness causes the problem; picturing a sculptor is forbidden, so one reads metaphorically or affirms without explaining.

outline.heading: A fistful of soil from the whole earth
outline.gist: He shares only the narrations with reasonable authenticity; whatever image comes to mind serves understanding, not a scientific account.

outline.heading: The colours of the earth and sixty cubits
outline.gist: Humans came in the earth's colours and temperaments, which can only be metaphorical; sixty cubits by whose arm is unknown, so there is no clash with fossils.

outline.heading: Iblis saw that Adam was hollow
outline.gist: The hollowness is the inner need and lack of fulfilment that makes us weak; Shaytan in the blood and his whispering to the deaf show these are not physical.

outline.heading: Why wage war on evolution?
outline.gist: These narrations were always read metaphorically, and a Muslim scholar a millennium ago described development from elements to microorganisms, fish, reptiles, animals and humans.

outline.heading: We did not come from monkeys
outline.gist: The theory posits shared ancestry with all life, which only arrogance finds offensive; kinship with creation is a reason to care for it.

outline.heading: Was Adam's garden on earth?
outline.gist: The Quranic verb for descent is used for moving from higher to lower land, as in going down to Egypt.

outline.heading: Why it was not the Paradise of the Hereafter
outline.gist: No one leaves Paradise, Iblis would not be there, and nothing is forbidden in it; he respects the opposing view.

outline.heading: A garden outside the food chain
outline.gist: Freed from survival, humans grew greedy and rebellious, as long-held instincts overpowered the command.

outline.heading: From nothing to something
outline.gist: Science does not study the origin of being from nothingness; that is Allah.

outline.heading: From lifelessness to life
outline.gist: The first cell's first breath, life from bare elements, is beyond science's reach.

outline.heading: Function: why life wants to live
outline.gist: Evolution assumes organisms want to survive and reproduce, but where did that drive come from? Allah gave life purpose and function.

outline.heading: Interlude
Guided or unguided evolution?
outline.gist: If we are here, the process was not unguided; programming that mutates randomly until it produces us is guidance by design.

outline.heading: Patterns need zooming out
outline.gist: Apparent randomness is often a pattern seen from too close.

outline.heading: Randomness by design is not chance
outline.gist: With far more mutations than possibilities, success is guaranteed, which is design; neither side has evidence about control of each mutation.

outline.heading: Reject it for science, not for religion
outline.gist: Oppose evolution on scientific grounds if you must; a single coded strand producing all life's diversity should inspire awe.

outline.heading: Outro

91SJ32gZZU8.one_line: The Prophet's bond with the Quran and his supplications: daily recitation, love of beautiful reading, and duas that were real conversations with Allah.
91SJ32gZZU8.summary: He continues the Prophet's worship with two subjects: the Quran and dua. The Prophet kept a daily portion of Quran he never missed, recited slowly and clearly, and loved hearing it from others, weeping when Ibn Mas'ud reached the verse about him as witness over his nation. He tells of Ubayy being named by Allah, the man who recited al-Ikhlas in every rakah out of love for its description of Allah, the surah's answer to those who asked for Allah's lineage, and Abu Musa's beautiful voice. He then goes through some of the Prophet's supplications: the dua for distress, his praise after Uhud, his testimony that all servants are brothers, the simple request for Jannah and refuge from the Fire, the rain prayer on the minbar, and the need for halal food for a dua to be answered. The heart of the talk is the dua at Ta'if, which he presents as a broken man pouring out his heart, only caring whether Allah was displeased. He contrasts this with reciting memorised words. He ends that the Quran is the Prophet's true legacy for this month, and that, like Ya'qub, believers should take every complaint to Allah rather than complaining about His decree.

outline.gist: The idolaters, who valued genealogy, asked for Allah's lineage and were answered with al-Ikhlas.

outline.heading: Abu Musa's voice
outline.gist: The Prophet listened to Abu Musa recite and told him he had a flute of the family of Dawud; Abu Musa wished he had known so he could do better.

outline.gist: Whoever does not recite melodiously is not of us, and the people of the Quran are Allah's special people.

outline.heading: The one with most Quran leads
outline.gist: Every travelling group needed a leader, chosen by who knew the most Quran.

outline.heading: His character was the Quran
outline.gist: Aisha described his manners simply as the Quran.

outline.heading: The dua for distress
outline.gist: I am Your servant, son of Your servants... make the Quran the spring of my heart; whoever says it, Allah relieves his worry.

outline.heading: Praise after Uhud
outline.gist: After Uhud he praised Allah as the One none can withhold what He gives, and asked that faith be made beloved and disbelief hateful.

outline.heading: All servants are brothers
outline.gist: He testified in his dua that Allah is Lord, he is His messenger, and all Allah's servants are brothers.

outline.heading: Jannah and refuge from the Fire
outline.gist: A farmer who left a long Isha behind Mu'adh said he only asks for Jannah and refuge from the Fire, and the Prophet said his own dua revolved around the same.

outline.heading: The rain prayer on the minbar
outline.gist: A man asked for rain during the Friday sermon; it rained for a week, then he asked that it fall around them and not on them.

outline.heading: Eat halal for an answered dua

outline.heading: Ta'if: the lowest moment
outline.gist: After losing Khadijah and Abu Talib and years of boycott, he was stoned out of Ta'if, bleeding, with Zayd watching.

outline.heading: The dua at Ta'if
outline.gist: He complained of his weakness to Allah and said nothing mattered as long as Allah was not angry with him, seeking refuge in the light of His face.

outline.heading: He felt what he said
outline.gist: We recite memorised duas, while he spoke what was in his heart; words like these could only come from a prophet.

outline.heading: Ibn Abbas hears his night dua
outline.gist: Staying at his aunt's house, Ibn Abbas heard him praise Allah as the light and sustainer of the heavens and earth and affirm every truth.

outline.heading: The Quran is his true legacy
outline.gist: He spent his life ensuring the book reached us and teaching how to live it; Ramadan is when it leaves the shelf and enters our lives.

outline.heading: Dua is a conversation: Ya'qub's complaint
outline.gist: Ya'qub, having lost his sons and his sight, said he takes his complaint only to Allah.

outline.heading: Complain to Him, not about Him
outline.gist: Life has ups and downs that are not personal; take every sorrow to Allah instead of objecting to His decree.

JOS7q3kMBqM.one_line: Opening the last ten: what the standing and the bowing in prayer are for, from al-Fatiha as a dialogue with Allah to the tasbih of ruku.
JOS7q3kMBqM.summary: On the first of the last ten nights the sheikh uses the breaks between rakaat to begin explaining what each position of the prayer is for. He starts with the standing. The best prayer is the one with long standing, and the standing is the place of the Quran. He explains the hadith qudsi in which Allah divides al-Fatiha between Himself and His servant and answers each verse: the praise, the glorification, the pledge to worship Him and seek His help, and the request for guidance, which Allah grants. He adds that Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz would pause after each verse to reflect on that answer, and that Allah faces the worshipper from the opening takbir until the worshipper turns away, while warning against picturing Allah like His creation. In the second reminder he moves to ruku. The Quran is not recited while bowing or prostrating, because the bow is for magnifying the Lord. He draws on the passage just recited, where 'Isa answers Allah's question with 'Glory be to You', as the model of tasbih, and closes with the words of glorification the Prophet said in ruku.

_Ufmg-94xvk.one_line: The Prophet as a devoted family man who served, played with and reconciled his household, and who treated animals with names, care and rights.
_Ufmg-94xvk.summary: He calls the Prophet the one who most succeeded in making family the core unit of a nation, and asks whether Muslims still guard it as they once did. Stories follow: racing Aisha, calmly gathering food from a plate broken in jealousy, Aisha searching for him at night, never letting a dispute last overnight, Abu Bakr walking in on an argument, standing for Aisha as she watched the Abyssinians, drinking from her cup during her period, playing with Hasan and Husayn even in sujud, honouring Fatimah, and bringing Ali home from the masjid floor. He speaks directly to men in the community who misunderstand their roles and abandon marriages too quickly, reminding them that the Prophet served at home, entered with a smile and held on through difficulty. He warns against pulling relatives into marital fights. Turning to animals, he notes that the Prophet named all his animals, grieved their loss, returned stolen eggs to a distressed bird, condemned branding faces and overworking, taught merciful slaughter, and posted a guard over a nursing dog. He closes that the Prophet treated animals almost as family, and that mocking people for loving pets does not reflect his way.

outline.gist: The two topics are paired only for scheduling.

outline.heading: Standing for Aisha at the Abyssinian display

outline.heading: Drinking from Aisha's cup during her period

outline.heading: Carrying Hasan and Husayn
outline.gist: He played with his grandchildren on his back and praised them as riders.

outline.heading: Lengthening sujud for his grandson
outline.gist: He stayed in prostration so the child on his back would not fall.

outline.heading: Honouring Fatimah
outline.gist: He rose for her, kissed her and seated her in his place, while telling his family early on that each must save themselves from the Fire.

outline.heading: Do not pull relatives into marital fights

outline.heading: Patience with an abusive uncle
outline.gist: Despite Abu Lahab's repeated harm, he never said a rude word to him because he was family.

outline.heading: He named all his animals
outline.gist: His donkey, camels and mule had names, and he was hurt when his camel was killed at Hudaybiyyah.

outline.heading: A cat, a pet bird and stolen eggs

outline.heading: Branding and overworking condemned
outline.gist: He cursed whoever branded a donkey's face and rebuked an owner for starving and overworking his camel.

outline.heading: Do not kill it twice
outline.gist: Sharpening the knife in front of an animal is forbidden; slaughter must be done properly and the animal used for food.

outline.heading: No target practice, no hunger

outline.heading: Al-Qaswa stops before Makkah
outline.gist: When companions said his camel was being stubborn, he defended her character: the One who held back the elephant held her back.

outline.heading: A guard for a nursing dog
outline.gist: On a narrow path he posted a companion so the army would not disturb a dog feeding her puppies.

outline.heading: Animals as part of the family
outline.gist: He loved and cared for his animals as partners on earth; mocking people for loving pets does not reflect his way.

g_VViSLj_y8.title: Facing Disbelief 2: The Universe as the First Source, and Anthropomorphism
g_VViSLj_y8.one_line: Answering five arguments against the universe as evidence for a Creator, then showing why the Quran's God is not the humanised straw man critics attack.
g_VViSLj_y8.summary: He takes the universe as the first source of eman, since the Quran repeatedly tells people to look at the heavens and earth. Belief rests on uniformity of evidence, every source pointing the same way, which gives more certainty than scientific proof with its margin of error. He then answers five arguments. The burden of proof falls on whoever denies a cause, because causality is a self-evident truth: universal, untaught, natural and simple, like the reality of the past or other minds; a prosecutor proves who killed, not that someone did. Russell's teapot fails because it explains nothing. The eternal universe is ruled out by thermodynamics and the Borde-Guth-Vilenkin theorem. The multiverse has no evidence, and Leslie's firing squad shows that luck is a poor explanation for life. Quantum virtual particles do not show something from nothing, since inability to measure is not absence and anything following a law cannot precede that law. In the second half he argues that many scientists reject a straw man: the humanised God of altered scriptures. The Quran insists nothing is like Allah; verbs and words like hand or Throne are given for human relevance and were either left unexplained or read metaphorically by scholars, never taken physically.

outline.heading: Opening
The universe as the first source of eman
outline.gist: The Quran's frequent command to look at the heavens and earth makes the universe the first source, and the sources must be taken in sequence.

outline.heading: Uniformity of evidence, not scientific proof
outline.gist: Science cannot reach beyond the observable universe, so belief rests on multiple independent sources pointing in one direction.

outline.heading: Why uniform evidence yields certainty
outline.gist: A single contrary source would collapse the case, yet all point to Allah; scientific proof, by contrast, always carries a margin of error.

outline.heading: Argument one: the burden of proof is on the believer
outline.gist: The claim that whoever asserts existence must prove it, since God is beyond the senses.

outline.heading: Self-evident truths and their four criteria
outline.gist: A self-evident truth is universal, untaught, natural and the simplest explanation.

outline.heading: Examples of self-evident truths
outline.gist: The existence of the past, other minds, the law of causality and basic logic are accepted by all without proof.

outline.heading: Denying a cause shifts the burden
outline.gist: Saying the universe has no cause restricts a self-evident truth, so the denier must prove causality does not apply.

outline.heading: The murder analogy
outline.gist: A prosecutor must prove who committed the murder, never that someone did; the details of who Allah is come later.

outline.heading: Argument two: Russell's teapot
outline.gist: The claim, popularised by Dawkins, that an undetectable teapot creator is as plausible as God.

outline.heading: Why the teapot explains nothing
outline.gist: Belief in a Creator answers why anything exists; a teapot answers nothing, and if it created the universe it is simply a creator by another name.

outline.heading: Argument three: an eternal universe
outline.gist: An ancient claim settled by science: an expanding universe governed by thermodynamics and the Borde-Guth-Vilenkin theorem must have a beginning.

outline.heading: Argument four: the multiverse
outline.gist: An idea with no evidence, popular only because scientists propose it; positing infinite universes is no less a leap than God.

outline.heading: Leslie's firing squad: the setup
outline.gist: The multiverse makes our existence a near-zero chance outcome; the Canadian philosopher John Leslie offers a thought experiment against this.

outline.heading: Luck or intent?
outline.gist: If fifty marksmen all miss, intent is the reasonable explanation; so too for a universe struck by the bullet of life.

outline.heading: The evidence keeps stacking one way
outline.gist: Faith draws on life, history and experience as well, and the multiverse has never communicated with anyone.

outline.heading: Argument five: the universe popped into existence
outline.gist: Dawkins and Krauss claim the universe simply appeared or created itself, leaning on quantum mechanics, which he studied in a university course.

outline.heading: Virtual particles
outline.gist: The claim that particles flicker in and out of existence, so existence needs no cause.

outline.heading: Not measured is not absent
outline.gist: The vacuum state may simply be beyond our tools, as breast cancer can be present while every blood test is normal.

outline.heading: Nothing can precede the law that governs it
outline.gist: If particles follow a law, the law preceded them; finely tuned gravity shows laws predating everything.

outline.heading: Quantum physics proves nothing about origins
outline.gist: Virtual particles are a phenomenon to research, not evidence that the universe came from nothing.

outline.heading: Seven heavens and no discrepancy
outline.gist: Seven in Arabic signifies endless repetition; the Quran invites us to see the uniformity of laws across creation.

outline.heading: The force behind existence is named Allah
outline.gist: Muslims do not start with a God and assign Him the role; they recognise a force behind existence and that force is Allah.

outline.heading: The straw man God scientists reject
outline.gist: Einstein, Darwin and others believed in a supreme power; what they rejected was the God of distorted scriptures, and Muslims are lumped in with it.

outline.heading: Anthropomorphism in altered scripture
outline.gist: The Old Testament and Bible depict God walking, wrestling and weeping, and Christians believe God bled on earth.

outline.heading: Why humans humanise God
outline.gist: People dislike being limited servants, so they either deify humans, as in superhero films, or bring God down to their level.

outline.heading: Idols and the wish for control
outline.gist: Idols that sit in the home let people feel they control their gods rather than serve them.

outline.heading: Nothing is like Him
outline.gist: He hears and sees, but not as we do; the verse of light likewise describes Him beyond human terms.

outline.heading: Fifteen descriptions in three verses
outline.gist: The First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden: only one beyond time and space fits these descriptions.

outline.heading: Divine actions in human words
outline.gist: Words for wrath, pleasure and rising over the Throne are used because a mind given nothing relatable cannot grasp Allah at all.

outline.heading: Under the umbrella of transcendence
outline.gist: Such words sit beneath the verses of transcendence; reading them without a sense of metaphor causes problems.

outline.heading: Hand and face: leaving the meaning or reading it as metaphor
outline.gist: The early scholars either left the meaning to Allah without asking or read hand as power and face as His self.

outline.heading: No scholar made them physical
outline.gist: No Muslim scholar ever said Allah has a physical hand, and it is forbidden even to gesture to one's own eye or hand when mentioning them.

outline.heading: The Throne and the Kursi
outline.gist: Asking to be given something relatable; for the Arabs the throne was the seat of command and the kursi the seat of knowledge, as with Imam Malik's chair.

outline.heading: Literalism and the hadith of Adam in His image
outline.gist: Metaphor-blind readers take hadith literally; the Quran never places God physically in the universe, unlike the Bible, and the image means the ethics man carries.

outline.heading: The hadith of the womb
outline.gist: Kinship clinging to Allah cannot be physical; its meaning is that Allah keeps ties with those who keep family ties.

outline.heading: Why the metaphors are there
outline.gist: The Quran itself requires the metaphorical reading; descriptions give relevance so we can connect, while we believe Allah transcends all of them.

outline.heading: Outro

oMQgLrJNR6I.title: Attributes of the Prophet: His Ease, Tenderness and Flexibility
oMQgLrJNR6I.one_line: The Prophet's mental flexibility in planning and leadership, and the ease and tenderness that made him a mercy to all creation.
oMQgLrJNR6I.summary: He takes two attributes together. Flexibility means accepting that life never goes as planned and adapting while holding firm to core values, which he credits for the ummah's long survival. He shows it in sending Muslims to Abyssinia as a second base, accepting al-Hubab's better camp site at Badr, going out to Uhud on the youths' vote and refusing to reverse once armoured, adopting Salman's trench at the Battle of the Trench and digging five kilometres through rock, accepting the lopsided terms of Hudaybiyyah for ten years of peace, and pairing Muhajirun with Ansar in shared homes. Muslims in today's unfamiliar context need the same open mind. On ease and tenderness, he cites the hadith that gentleness beautifies everything, the mercy shown at Ta'if when the angel of the mountains offered to crush his persecutors, and his prayer for his people at Uhud despite his wounds. He describes how the Prophet treated young students of knowledge, held back from commands like siwak at every prayer to avoid hardship, shortened prayer for a crying child, rebuked a man who never kissed his children, and comforted the weeping palm trunk. He ends that the Prophet was not just merciful but sent as mercy itself.

outline.heading: Opening
Flexibility: life will not go as planned
outline.gist: Mental flexibility means adapting to circumstances while holding on to core values; it is why the ummah has survived so long.

outline.heading: Abyssinia as a second base
outline.gist: Sending Muslims across the sea to a foreign land so Islam would survive was out-of-the-box thinking he saw through for fifteen years.

outline.heading: Al-Hubab changes the camp at Badr
outline.gist: When a companion said the camp site was poor strategy, the Prophet immediately adopted his better plan to control the wells; he did similar on another campaign.

outline.heading: Uhud: following the majority
outline.gist: He preferred to defend Madinah but went out on the youths' vote, and refused to reverse once he had put on his armour.

outline.heading: Salman's trench proposal
outline.gist: Outnumbered heavily, the companions laughed at a foreign former slave's idea, but the Prophet took it seriously.

outline.heading: Digging the trench through rock
outline.gist: A five-kilometre trench across Madinah's only open approach, each companion digging a bedroom's volume in ten days with hand tools.

outline.heading: Changing plans at Hudaybiyyah
outline.gist: The plan shifted from umrah to fighting and back as the rumour of Uthman's death came and went, and the companions adapted each time.

outline.heading: Accepting an unjust treaty
outline.gist: He accepted humiliating terms, erasing his own title, for ten years of peace.

outline.heading: The brotherhood of Muhajirun and Ansar
outline.gist: Pairing strangers from different cities to share homes was thought impossible, and people came just to see it.

outline.heading: Flexibility for Muslims today
outline.gist: Living in a place and era with few parallels to where we came from, Muslims need open minds to reach their goals.

outline.heading: Gentleness beautifies everything
outline.gist: Ease adorns anything it enters and its absence disfigures; the merciful are shown mercy by the Most Merciful.

outline.heading: Ta'if and the angel of the mountains
outline.gist: On the worst day of his life, rejected and wandering, he refused to have his persecutors crushed and hoped for believers among their descendants.

outline.heading: Praying for his people at Uhud
outline.gist: Wounded and bleeding, he raised his hands and the companions feared a curse, but he prayed for his people's forgiveness, as an earlier prophet had.

outline.heading: Tenderness with young students
outline.gist: Malik ibn al-Huwayrith's group of youths was asked about their families and sent home kindly to teach and lead their people in prayer.

outline.heading: Students are the Prophet's trust
outline.gist: Companions welcomed young learners as those the Prophet told them to care for; masajid should do the same.

outline.heading: Holding back to avoid hardship
outline.gist: He did not command siwak at every prayer or make some acts obligatory, so as not to burden his ummah.

outline.heading: Shortening prayer for a crying child
outline.gist: He would cut a long prayer short on hearing a child cry, thinking of the mother.

outline.heading: The man who never kissed his children
outline.gist: He told him he could do nothing if Allah had removed mercy from his heart.

outline.heading: The weeping palm trunk
outline.gist: When he moved to the new minbar, the trunk he used to lean on cried until he came down and embraced it.

outline.heading: Sent as mercy itself
outline.gist: Other qualities describe him, but with mercy he is identified with it: sent only as a mercy to the worlds.

outline.heading: Outro

B2iD4vRyI0E.speaker: adnan
B2iD4vRyI0E.speaker_note: single speaker continuing his Ramadan morning series on the Prophet's attributes
B2iD4vRyI0E.title: Attributes of the Prophet: His Loyalty
B2iD4vRyI0E.one_line: Wafa in the Prophet's life: never forgetting good done to him, repaying it, and keeping his word to the end whatever it cost.
B2iD4vRyI0E.summary: He defines wafa as never forgetting a kindness done to you and working to repay it, which carries trustworthiness and loyalty within it. People naturally remember the good they did and the harm done to them; wafa reverses that. He traces it through the Prophet's life: rewarding al-Arqam for his house, the special standing of the people of Badr that saved Hatib, constant remembrance of the martyrs of Uhud, weeping at his mother's grave. He dwells on Aminah's journey to Madinah so her son would know his late father's family, and uses it to challenge parents who cut children off from the other parent's relatives, since children need their family for stability. Abu Talib protected him for life because he gave his word to his father. The Prophet honoured Halimah and freed his foster siblings, said he had repaid everyone except Abu Bakr, kept his pledge to the Ansar by living and being buried in Madinah rather than his beloved Makkah, and ordered that Abu al-Bakhtari be spared at Badr for ending the boycott. Even when it broke his heart, he returned Abu Jandal at Hudaybiyyah because he had given his word. He closes that keeping one's word is basic human decency, and without it little else we claim is worth much.

outline.heading: What wafa means
outline.gist: Never forgetting a good deed done for you and trying to repay it; it contains trustworthiness and loyalty.

outline.heading: Repaying al-Arqam for his house
outline.gist: He publicly gave al-Arqam a valuable sword from the spoils as thanks for hosting the early Muslims in Makkah.

outline.heading: Reverse what we naturally remember
outline.gist: We easily recall the good we did and the harm done to us; wafa means remembering others' kindness and our own faults instead.

outline.heading: The people of Badr and Hatib's letter
outline.gist: Hatib's warning letter to Quraysh was a grave mistake, yet he was forgiven because of the standing of those who stood by the Prophet at Badr.

outline.heading: Remembering the martyrs of Uhud
outline.gist: He lost key companions like Mus'ab and Hamzah at Uhud and kept visiting and praying for them by name until the end of his life.

outline.heading: Weeping at his mother's grave
outline.gist: He wept at Aminah's grave and was allowed to visit but not to seek forgiveness for her, and told people to visit graves to remember death.

outline.heading: Aminah's journey to Madinah
outline.gist: Out of loyalty to her late husband, she travelled 400 km so her son would know his father's relatives, and died on the way back.

outline.heading: Let children know both families
outline.gist: Parents who cut children off from the other parent's family weaken them; every child needs their blood relatives for stability.

outline.heading: A childhood visit that paved the hijrah
outline.gist: He learned to swim in Madinah at six, and the relatives who remembered him welcomed him years later.

outline.heading: Abu Talib keeps his word to his father
outline.gist: Abu Talib protected the Prophet all his life because he promised Abd al-Muttalib, and the Prophet in turn raised Ali and cared for Ja'far.

outline.heading: Halimah smiling in the crowd
outline.gist: He recognised his elderly wet nurse while distributing spoils and spent a long time with her.

outline.heading: Freeing his foster siblings
outline.gist: When Halimah's children were among the captives, he gave up his share and asked others to free them by their choice.

outline.heading: The debt he could not repay Abu Bakr
outline.gist: He repaid everyone except Abu Bakr, left his reward to Allah, and kept only Abu Bakr's door into the masjid open.

outline.heading: He reminded people of their favours
outline.gist: Abu Bakr disliked hearing it, but the Prophet kept mentioning good done to him, while we should forget the good we do for others.

outline.heading: The pledge to the Ansar
outline.gist: When the Ansar feared being abandoned after victory, he promised their blood was his blood and he would be with them in life and death.

outline.heading: Living and buried in Madinah
outline.gist: Though Makkah was his ancestral home and love, he returned to Madinah after the conquest and was buried there to keep his word.

outline.heading: The man who ended the boycott
outline.gist: Abu al-Bakhtari helped tear up the Quraysh boycott that starved Banu Hashim for three years.

outline.heading: Spare Abu al-Bakhtari at Badr
outline.gist: Out of loyalty the Prophet ordered him spared, but he insisted on fighting and was killed, leaving the companion distressed.

outline.heading: Abu Jandal returned at Hudaybiyyah
outline.gist: Abu Jandal escaped to the Muslims as his own father signed the clause requiring his return; the Prophet pleaded but kept his word and sent him back.

outline.heading: If your word is not good
outline.gist: Keeping your word to the end, even after the other person is gone, is basic decency, honesty and grit; without it little good remains.

28:9.en: And the wife of Pharaoh said: (He will be) a consolation for me and for thee. Kill him not. Peradventure he may be of use to us, or we may choose him for a son. And they perceived not

PUanNK1azLk.speaker: adnan
PUanNK1azLk.speaker_note: leads the nightly reflections, recalls praying at the Kaaba as a child while his father worked in the Haram, refers to his own surah summaries
PUanNK1azLk.title: Ramadan 2023, Night 19: Quranic Reflections (Al-Naml to Al-Ankabut)
PUanNK1azLk.one_line: Opening the cluster on relationships: 'what were you doing?', not judging Musa's mother, not forcing guidance, acting for Allah's Face, and the certainty of tests.
PUanNK1azLk.summary: He finishes the cluster on carrying the message and opens a new one, al-Qasas to al-Sajdah, on relationships: with people, life, Allah's laws, generations and Allah. The question on Judgment Day, 'or what were you doing?', terrifies him: like an employer who already knows the cashier is stealing, Allah asks only to let us account for how we spent a life He gave a clear purpose. Al-Qasas teaches that every story has more than one telling. Anyone watching Musa's mother cast her baby into the Nile would condemn her, yet Allah steadied her emptied heart and returned her son to her, paid by Pharaoh. So stop judging people, family most of all, because you barely know yourself. The verse revealed over Abu Talib, and his own grandmother's death, show that we cannot force guidance on those we love; we teach, mentor and offer it humbly, then leave it to Allah. Everything perishes but Allah's Face, so within a century we will all be forgotten, and only what is done for Him remains, as with the sheep the Prophet gave away. Al-Ankabut opens by promising that every claim of faith will be tested, so keep that verse ready for hardship.

outline.heading: Recap: the cluster on carrying the message
outline.gist: Responsibility, the Quran as tool, family, fulfilment, role models, investing in people, the journey, protecting society, then the effects of bad company, narrative and power.

outline.heading: A new cluster on relationships: al-Qasas
outline.gist: From al-Qasas the surahs each take a type of relationship; al-Qasas deals with people and the fact that every story can be told more than one way.

outline.heading: Relationships with life, Allah's laws, generations and Allah
outline.gist: Al-Ankabut takes our relationship with what life deals us, then the laws of the universe, the generations, and Allah Himself.

outline.heading: Interlude
The verse he heard as a boy at the Kaaba
outline.gist: Praying in front of the Kaaba as a child, he heard this verse recited and it has stayed with him as one of the heaviest in the Quran.

outline.heading: Power carries the message, yet you are weak
outline.gist: Al-Naml shows people do not follow the weak, so dawah needs strength in every form, but the end of the surah reminds us how weak we really are.

outline.heading: Did you deny My signs without knowledge?
outline.gist: On Judgment Day Allah asks whether people rejected His signs without studying or reflecting on them, only because they did not suit them.

outline.heading: Or what were you doing? The cashier example
outline.gist: Like an owner who has watched the cashier pocket money, the question is asked when the answer is already known, to let the person account for himself.

outline.heading: Nothing left to explain
outline.gist: There is nothing anyone could say to Allah to justify what he brings; he says he fears this question.

outline.heading: Walk me through your day
outline.gist: A father finds none of his son's tasks done and asks for an hour-by-hour account; Allah made our purpose and method clear and will ask how we spent our lives.

outline.heading: Only you can tell your own story
outline.gist: A large part of relating to people is accepting that others see the same events through a different lens; al-Qasas opens with Musa's mother to show it.

outline.heading: The reciter who chose a verse for the oppressed
outline.gist: After the occupation of Palestine an Egyptian reciter, among the first to recite publicly there, chose Allah's promise to make the oppressed leaders and inheritors, showing real sensitivity to the moment.

outline.heading: Musa's mother casts him into the Nile
outline.gist: Told in a dream to float her son on the Nile, she did something any onlooker would have condemned.

outline.heading: Stop judging people
outline.gist: We act as if we have the tools to judge others' mistakes and struggles; we do not, and we should stop immediately.

outline.heading: You do not know your own family
outline.gist: Siblings raised in the same house differ in makeup, experiences and how they felt their parents' treatment, so quick judgment ruins family ties.

outline.heading: Her heart became empty
outline.gist: Her grief drained her completely and she almost gave him away, until Allah held her heart steady so she could remain a believer.

outline.heading: The heart of a mother
outline.gist: Men cannot grasp a mother's bond with her son; a father's love, as with Yaqub, is beautiful but different.

outline.heading: Pharaoh pays her to nurse her own son
outline.gist: He refused every wet nurse, his sister pointed them to his mother, and the king who wanted him dead returned him to her; be very careful before you judge.

outline.heading: Interlude
You cannot guide whom you love
outline.gist: The one thing we most wish we could do is secure guidance for those we love, and the verse says we cannot.

outline.heading: The Prophet pleads with Abu Talib
outline.gist: The link of the verse to the story is debated, but the Prophet begged the uncle who raised and protected him for one word and, as far as we can tell, did not get it.

outline.heading: Allah guides those who want guidance
outline.gist: The verse consoles the Prophet: guidance is Allah's, and loving someone without iman is heart-wrenching.

outline.heading: The grief of a loved one dying without faith
outline.gist: His maternal grandmother died, as far as he knows, without accepting Islam, and that grief differed from every other loss; feel for those who carry it.

outline.heading: Our part: teach, inspire, mentor
outline.gist: All we can do is educate, train and support; not knowing where our role ends harms us.

outline.heading: Offer guidance humbly and keep trying
outline.gist: Do not give up, but our own guidance is Allah's gift, so offer it in an attractive package and, if refused, ask whether you offered it well.

outline.heading: Everything perishes except His Face
outline.gist: There is no god but Him and everything will cease to exist; His Face is the Arabic way of referring to Him.

outline.heading: Allah is outside the time He created
outline.gist: He has no beginning or end, and trying to fit God into time, something He made, is foolish.

outline.heading: In a hundred years no one here will remain
outline.gist: By 2123 everyone in the room will be gone and forgotten; few know even their great-grandparents' names.

outline.heading: Do it for the Face of Allah
outline.gist: Anything done for people dies with them; what is given to Allah lives on because He never ceases.

outline.heading: What remains is what we give away
outline.gist: When the Prophet gave away a slaughtered sheep, he told Aisha that all of it remained except the shoulder they would eat.

outline.heading: Al-Ankabut: did people think they would not be tested?
outline.gist: The surah on our relationship with life opens without introduction on a verse everyone should carry in the heart.

outline.heading: Allah will expose who is truthful
outline.gist: Those before were tested, and saying you believe means preparing for what is coming.

outline.heading: There is no smooth sailing
outline.gist: Life is one challenge after another for the poorest and richest alike, and a claim of faith must be tested.

outline.heading: Your Lord answers your Fatiha: we will see
outline.gist: Each time you declare that you worship and seek help only from Him, Allah answers, and the tests show whether it was true.

outline.heading: Pull this verse out in hardship
outline.gist: Tests will come in faith, wealth and health; when they do, recall the verse and ask Allah for tests you can pass.

outline.heading: Outro

11:114.ar: وَأَقِمِ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ طَرَفَيِ ٱلنَّهَارِ وَزُلَفࣰ ا مِّنَ ٱلَّيۡلِۚ إِنَّ ٱلۡحَسَنَٰتِ يُذۡهِبۡنَ ٱلسَّيِّـَٔاتِۚ ذَٰلِكَ ذِكۡرَىٰ لِلذَّٰكِرِينَ

17:78.ar: أَقِمِ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ لِدُلُوكِ ٱلشَّمۡسِ إِلَىٰ غَسَقِ ٱلَّيۡلِ وَقُرۡءَانَ ٱلۡفَجۡرِۖ إِنَّ قُرۡءَانَ ٱلۡفَجۡرِ كَانَ مَشۡهُودࣰ ا
17:78.en: Establish worship at the going down of the sun until the dark of night, and (the recital of) the Qur'an at dawn. Lo! (the recital of) the Qur'an at dawn is ever witnessed

20:14.ar: إِنَّنِيٓ أَنَا ٱللَّهُ لَآ إِلَٰهَ إِلَّآ أَنَا۠ فَٱعۡبُدۡنِي وَأَقِمِ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ لِذِكۡرِيٓ
20:14.en: Lo! I, even I, am Allah, There is no Allah save Me. So serve Me and establish worship for My remembrance

73:1.en: O thou wrapped up in thy raiment

73:2.en: Keep vigil the night long, save a little

73:4.ar: أَوۡ زِدۡ عَلَيۡهِ وَرَتِّلِ ٱلۡقُرۡءَانَ تَرۡتِيلًا
73:4.en: Or add (a little) thereto - and chant the Qur'an in measure

33:35.ar: إِنَّ ٱلۡمُسۡلِمِينَ وَٱلۡمُسۡلِمَٰتِ وَٱلۡمُؤۡمِنِينَ وَٱلۡمُؤۡمِنَٰتِ وَٱلۡقَٰنِتِينَ وَٱلۡقَٰنِتَٰتِ وَٱلصَّٰدِقِينَ وَٱلصَّٰدِقَٰتِ وَٱلصَّٰبِرِينَ وَٱلصَّٰبِرَٰتِ وَٱلۡخَٰشِعِينَ وَٱلۡخَٰشِعَٰتِ وَٱلۡمُتَصَدِّقِينَ وَٱلۡمُتَصَدِّقَٰتِ وَٱلصَّٰٓئِمِينَ وَٱلصَّٰٓئِمَٰتِ وَٱلۡحَٰفِظِينَ فُرُوجَهُمۡ وَٱلۡحَٰفِظَٰتِ وَٱلذَّٰكِرِينَ ٱللَّهَ كَثِيرࣰ ا وَٱلذَّٰكِرَٰتِ أَعَدَّ ٱللَّهُ لَهُم مَّغۡفِرَةࣰ وَأَجۡرًا عَظِيمࣰ ا
33:35.en: Lo! men who surrender unto Allah, and women who surrender, and men who believe and women who believe, and men who obey and women who obey, and men who speak the truth and women who speak the truth, and men who persevere (in righteousness) and women who persevere, and men who are humble and women who are humble, and men who give alms and women who give alms, and men who fast and women who fast, and men who guard their modesty and women who guard (their modesty), and men who remember Allah much and women who remember - Allah hath prepared for them forgiveness and a vast reward

dYEOPnXlRuY.speaker: adnan
dYEOPnXlRuY.speaker_note: single speaker continuing his Ramadan series on the Prophet's attributes
dYEOPnXlRuY.title: Attributes of the Prophet: His Worship, Part 1
dYEOPnXlRuY.one_line: The Prophet's salah and dhikr: prayer as his refuge and joy, long night prayer as training, and a tongue always moist with remembrance.
dYEOPnXlRuY.summary: He pairs prayer and remembrance because the Quran makes remembrance the purpose of salah. The Prophet found rest in prayer, ran to it when distressed, and from the first revelations was told to stand the night, which he did for hours every night of his life, while today's worshippers complain about ninety minutes of taraweeh. He stresses moving from praying because you must to praying because you want to. He covers the man told three times to repeat his prayer until he learned calm in each position, and the river hadith of the five prayers. He then argues that obligatory congregational prayers must be kept short, as Mu'adh was rebuked for, but sunnah prayers such as taraweeh exist to train people, so trimming them to please the crowd does them no favour. Companions' accounts of his long night prayers, his answer that he wanted to be a grateful servant, and Rabi'ah's request to accompany him in Jannah through much prostration follow. On dhikr, he cites the hadith on the best of deeds, the forerunners who remember Allah often, and the bedouin told to keep his tongue moist with remembrance. He explains the Prophet's hundred daily istighfar as heightened sensitivity to falling short, and urges everyone to keep a fixed daily portion of dhikr.

outline.heading: Prayer for the sake of remembrance
outline.gist: Verses on establishing prayer at the ends of the day and night, ending with prayer established for Allah's remembrance, which is why salah and dhikr belong together.

outline.heading: Give us rest through it, Bilal
outline.gist: Muslims repeat that the Prophet loved prayer and found serenity in it, but rarely take that further themselves.

outline.heading: Running to prayer when distressed
outline.gist: Whenever something troubled him, prayer was where he went for relief.

outline.heading: Stand the night: the early command
outline.gist: Among the first revelations was the instruction to the one wrapped in garments to pray much of the night and recite with care.

outline.heading: Six hours versus ninety minutes
outline.gist: He prayed for hours nightly all his life, while people today complain when taraweeh runs a few minutes longer.

outline.heading: From having to, to wanting to
outline.gist: He became like a different person when prayer came; worship begins as duty and, done right, becomes something you cannot live without.

outline.heading: Praising his Lord after Uhud
outline.gist: After that devastating day, he lined the companions up behind him to praise and thank Allah.

outline.heading: The man who prayed badly
outline.gist: Sent back three times, the man was taught to settle calmly in every position rather than racing through.

outline.heading: The river at your door
outline.gist: Five daily prayers done properly wash away sins like bathing in a river five times a day.

outline.heading: Sunnah is for training, not pleasing
outline.gist: An imam should not lengthen obligatory prayers, but shrinking sunnah prayers like taraweeh to please people fails to train them to stand before Allah.

outline.heading: Mu'adh rebuked for a long fard
outline.gist: Mu'adh was told he was causing fitnah by lengthening Isha; obligatory prayers are to be concise because people must get on with their lives.

outline.heading: Companions praying behind him at night
outline.gist: Companions who joined his night prayer were exhausted by its length, while for him it was his joy.

outline.heading: Shall I not be a grateful servant?
outline.gist: Asked why he strained when all his sins were forgiven, he said he wished to be thankful.

outline.heading: The time for sleep is gone
outline.gist: In the early days he told Khadijah that his time of sleep was over.

outline.heading: Ibn Abbas counts thirteen rakat
outline.gist: Ibn Abbas watched him pray long pairs of rakat, each shorter than the last, totalling thirteen.

outline.heading: Rabi'ah at his doorstep
outline.gist: The young servant slept at his door and heard him praying and praising all night, then was told to ask for anything.

outline.heading: Help me with much prostration
outline.gist: Rabi'ah asked to be with him in Jannah, and the Prophet asked him to help by praying a great deal.

outline.heading: The best of deeds is dhikr
outline.gist: Remembrance outweighs spending wealth and fighting, and it is the one worship that continues in Jannah, so the tongue must get used to it now.

outline.heading: The forerunners
outline.gist: Passing a mountain on the road to Makkah, he said the mufarridun had gone ahead: men and women who remember Allah much.

outline.heading: Keep your tongue moist
outline.gist: A man overwhelmed by Islam's many rulings asked for one thing to hold on to and was told to keep his tongue moist with remembrance.

outline.heading: A hundred istighfar a day
outline.gist: He sought forgiveness a hundred times whenever he felt a lapse in focus.

outline.heading: Sensitivity to sin
outline.gist: The more sensitive the heart, the more it sees its shortfalls; feeling no sin at all is itself something to seek forgiveness for.

outline.heading: A treasure of Jannah
outline.gist: He taught a short phrase called a treasure of Jannah and a hundred daily glorifications; a counter takes two minutes.

outline.heading: Keep a daily portion of dhikr
outline.gist: A Muslim needs a fixed daily amount of remembrance, during commutes or before sleep, that is never dropped.

outline.heading: How much of my dua should be for you?
outline.gist: A companion asked how much of his invocation to devote to sending blessings on the Prophet, and was encouraged to give more.

17:44.ar: تُسَبِّحُ لَهُ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتُ ٱلسَّبۡعُ وَٱلۡأَرۡضُ وَمَن فِيهِنَّۚ وَإِن مِّن شَيۡءٍ إِلَّا يُسَبِّحُ بِحَمۡدِهِۦ وَلَٰكِن لَّا تَفۡقَهُونَ تَسۡبِيحَهُمۡۚ إِنَّهُۥ كَانَ حَلِيمًا غَفُورࣰ ا
17:44.en: The seven heavens and the earth and all that is therein praise Him, and there is not a thing but hymneth His praise; but ye understand not their praise. Lo! He is ever Clement, Forgiving

14:34.ar: وَءَاتَىٰكُم مِّن كُلِّ مَا سَأَلۡتُمُوهُۚ وَإِن تَعُدُّواْ نِعۡمَتَ ٱللَّهِ لَا تُحۡصُوهَآۗ إِنَّ ٱلۡإِنسَٰنَ لَظَلُومࣱ كَفَّارࣱ‏
14:34.en: And He giveth you of all ye ask of Him, and if ye would count the bounty of Allah ye cannot reckon it. Lo! man is verily a wrong-doer, an ingrate

hFwHhnnOg6g.speaker: adnan
hFwHhnnOg6g.speaker_note: Tahajjud night on his own channel from his masjid; he leads the prayer and gives the reminders between rakaat, no one else is introduced.
hFwHhnnOg6g.title: Ramadan 2023, Night 22: Tahajjud
hFwHhnnOg6g.one_line: Between rakaat: the meaning of ruku, rising from it and sujud, with Dawud's lesson that even thanking Allah is His gift.
hFwHhnnOg6g.summary: Night twenty-two takes the congregation through the next positions of the prayer in two reminders between sets of rakaat. In the first, the sheikh stays with the bowing. He explains the Prophet's dua in ruku, in which hearing, sight, brain, bones and sinews all humble themselves to Allah, and links it to the verse that everything in creation glorifies Allah's praise even though people do not grasp how. He dwells on the glorification of the Lord the Magnificent, then on rising from ruku: Allah hears whoever praises Him, and the worshipper answers with a praise that fills the heavens and the earth and admits that no one can hold back what Allah gives or give what He withholds. In the second reminder he turns to gratitude. Allah's favours cannot be counted, and he tells how Dawud asked how he could ever thank Allah when his thanks was itself a favour from Him, and was told that now he had thanked Him. He then brings the worshipper down into prostration with the takbir: the place to multiply dua because it is likely to be answered, where a servant is closest to his Lord, glorifying the Most High.

outline.gist: He explains the Prophet's words in ruku: to You I bowed, in You I believed, and my hearing, sight, brain, bones and sinews are humbled before You.

outline.heading: All creation glorifies Allah

outline.heading: Glory to my Lord the Magnificent
outline.gist: He dwells on the tasbih of ruku and what it means to glorify the Lord as Magnificent.

outline.heading: Rising from ruku: Allah hears the one who praises Him
outline.gist: He explains the words on rising and the long praise that fills the heavens and earth and confesses that none can withhold what Allah gives.

Allah's favours cannot be counted

outline.heading: Dawud: even thanking Allah is His gift
outline.gist: Dawud asked how he could thank Allah when his thanks was itself a blessing, and Allah told him that this recognition was his thanks.

outline.heading: Going down into sujud with the takbir
outline.gist: He describes how the Prophet rose from ruku, said the takbir and went down into prostration.

outline.heading: Make much dua in sujud
outline.gist: The Prophet told his companions to strive in dua while prostrating because it is likely to be answered.

outline.heading: Closest to Allah in prostration
outline.gist: A servant is nearest to his Lord while in sujud, so it is the moment to ask.

outline.heading: Glory to my Lord the Most High
outline.gist: He closes on the tasbih of sujud, glorifying Allah as the Most High.

If you tried to count Allah's favours you could not number them (the same words open 16:18): the basis for his talk on gratitude.

hadith.gist: The Prophet's dua in ruku: to You I have bowed, in You I believe, to You I submit; my hearing, sight, brain, bones and sinews are humbled before You.

takeaways: Say the dua of ruku and mean it: every part of you bowing to Allah.
When rising from ruku, praise Allah fully, knowing He hears it.
Admit you can never thank Allah enough; that admission is itself gratitude.

29:46.ar: ۞وَلَا تُجَٰدِلُوٓاْ أَهۡلَ ٱلۡكِتَٰبِ إِلَّا بِٱلَّتِي هِيَ أَحۡسَنُ إِلَّا ٱلَّذِينَ ظَلَمُواْ مِنۡهُمۡۖ وَقُولُوٓاْ ءَامَنَّا بِٱلَّذِيٓ أُنزِلَ إِلَيۡنَا وَأُنزِلَ إِلَيۡكُمۡ وَإِلَٰهُنَا وَإِلَٰهُكُمۡ وَٰحِدࣱ وَنَحۡنُ لَهُۥ مُسۡلِمُونَ
29:46.en: And argue not with the People of the Scripture unless it be in (a way) that is better, save with such of them as do wrong; and say: We believe in that which hath been revealed unto us and revealed unto you; our Allah and your Allah is One, and unto Him we surrender

30:3.ar: فِيٓ أَدۡنَى ٱلۡأَرۡضِ وَهُم مِّنۢ بَعۡدِ غَلَبِهِمۡ سَيَغۡلِبُونَ
30:3.en: In the nearer land, and they, after their defeat will be victorious

30:4.ar: فِي بِضۡعِ سِنِينَۗ لِلَّهِ ٱلۡأَمۡرُ مِن قَبۡلُ وَمِنۢ بَعۡدُۚ وَيَوۡمَئِذࣲ يَفۡرَحُ ٱلۡمُؤۡمِنُونَ
30:4.en: Within ten years - Allah's is the command in the former case and in the latter - and in that day believers will rejoice

30:5.ar: بِنَصۡرِ ٱللَّهِۚ يَنصُرُ مَن يَشَآءُۖ وَهُوَ ٱلۡعَزِيزُ ٱلرَّحِيمُ
30:5.en: In Allah's help to victory. He helpeth to victory whom He will. He is the Mighty, the Merciful

30:30.ar: فَأَقِمۡ وَجۡهَكَ لِلدِّينِ حَنِيفࣰ اۚ فِطۡرَتَ ٱللَّهِ ٱلَّتِي فَطَرَ ٱلنَّاسَ عَلَيۡهَاۚ لَا تَبۡدِيلَ لِخَلۡقِ ٱللَّهِۚ ذَٰلِكَ ٱلدِّينُ ٱلۡقَيِّمُ وَلَٰكِنَّ أَكۡثَرَ ٱلنَّاسِ لَا يَعۡلَمُونَ
30:30.en: So set thy purpose (O Muhammad) for religion as a man by nature upright - the nature (framed) of Allah, in which He hath created man. There is no altering (the laws of) Allah's creation. That is the right religion, but most men know not

30:54.ar: ۞ٱللَّهُ ٱلَّذِي خَلَقَكُم مِّن ضَعۡفࣲ ثُمَّ جَعَلَ مِنۢ بَعۡدِ ضَعۡفࣲ قُوَّةࣰ ثُمَّ جَعَلَ مِنۢ بَعۡدِ قُوَّةࣲ ضَعۡفࣰ ا وَشَيۡبَةࣰۚ يَخۡلُقُ مَا يَشَآءُۚ وَهُوَ ٱلۡعَلِيمُ ٱلۡقَدِيرُ
30:54.en: Allah is He Who shaped you out of weakness, then appointed after weakness strength, then, after strength, appointed weakness and grey hair. He createth what He will. He is the Knower, the Mighty

31:18.ar: وَلَا تُصَعِّرۡ خَدَّكَ لِلنَّاسِ وَلَا تَمۡشِ فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ مَرَحًاۖ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يُحِبُّ كُلَّ مُخۡتَالࣲ فَخُورࣲ‏
31:18.en: Turn not thy cheek in scorn toward folk, nor walk with pertness in the land. Lo! Allah loveth not each braggart boaster

32:15.ar: إِنَّمَا يُؤۡمِنُ بِـَٔايَٰتِنَا ٱلَّذِينَ إِذَا ذُكِّرُواْ بِهَا خَرُّواْۤ سُجَّدࣰ اۤ وَسَبَّحُواْ بِحَمۡدِ رَبِّهِمۡ وَهُمۡ لَا يَسۡتَكۡبِرُونَ۩
32:15.en: Only those believe in Our revelations who, when they are reminded of them, fall down prostrate and hymn the praise of their Lord, and they are not scornful

32:16.ar: تَتَجَافَىٰ جُنُوبُهُمۡ عَنِ ٱلۡمَضَاجِعِ يَدۡعُونَ رَبَّهُمۡ خَوۡفࣰ ا وَطَمَعࣰ ا وَمِمَّا رَزَقۡنَٰهُمۡ يُنفِقُونَ
32:16.en: Who forsake their beds to cry unto their Lord in fear and hope, and spend of that We have bestowed on them

32:21.ar: وَلَنُذِيقَنَّهُم مِّنَ ٱلۡعَذَابِ ٱلۡأَدۡنَىٰ دُونَ ٱلۡعَذَابِ ٱلۡأَكۡبَرِ لَعَلَّهُمۡ يَرۡجِعُونَ
32:21.en: And verily We make them taste the lower punishment before the greater, that haply they may return

33:21.ar: لَّقَدۡ كَانَ لَكُمۡ فِي رَسُولِ ٱللَّهِ أُسۡوَةٌ حَسَنَةࣱ لِّمَن كَانَ يَرۡجُواْ ٱللَّهَ وَٱلۡيَوۡمَ ٱلۡأٓخِرَ وَذَكَرَ ٱللَّهَ كَثِيرࣰ ا
33:21.en: Verily in the messenger of Allah ye have a good example for him who looketh unto Allah and the Last Day, and remembereth Allah much

33:22.ar: وَلَمَّا رَءَا ٱلۡمُؤۡمِنُونَ ٱلۡأَحۡزَابَ قَالُواْ هَٰذَا مَا وَعَدَنَا ٱللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُۥ وَصَدَقَ ٱللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُۥۚ وَمَا زَادَهُمۡ إِلَّآ إِيمَٰنࣰ ا وَتَسۡلِيمࣰ ا
33:22.en: And when the true believers saw the clans, they said: This is that which Allah and His messenger promised us. Allah and His messenger are true. It did but confirm them in their faith and resignation

26:17.en: (Saying): Let the Children of Israel go with us

3:140.ar: إِن يَمۡسَسۡكُمۡ قَرۡحࣱ فَقَدۡ مَسَّ ٱلۡقَوۡمَ قَرۡحࣱ مِّثۡلُهُۥۚ وَتِلۡكَ ٱلۡأَيَّامُ نُدَاوِلُهَا بَيۡنَ ٱلنَّاسِ وَلِيَعۡلَمَ ٱللَّهُ ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ وَيَتَّخِذَ مِنكُمۡ شُهَدَآءَۗ وَٱللَّهُ لَا يُحِبُّ ٱلظَّٰلِمِينَ
3:140.en: If ye have received a blow, the (disbelieving) people have received a blow the like thereof. These are (only) the vicissitudes which We cause to follow one another for mankind, to the end that Allah may know those who believe and may choose witnesses from among you; and Allah loveth not wrong-doers

62:2.ar: هُوَ ٱلَّذِي بَعَثَ فِي ٱلۡأُمِّيِّـۧنَ رَسُولࣰ ا مِّنۡهُمۡ يَتۡلُواْ عَلَيۡهِمۡ ءَايَٰتِهِۦ وَيُزَكِّيهِمۡ وَيُعَلِّمُهُمُ ٱلۡكِتَٰبَ وَٱلۡحِكۡمَةَ وَإِن كَانُواْ مِن قَبۡلُ لَفِي ضَلَٰلࣲ مُّبِينࣲ‏
62:2.en: He it is Who hath sent among the unlettered ones a messenger of their own, to recite unto them His revelations and to make them grow, and to teach them the Scripture and wisdom, though heretofore they were indeed in error manifest

FI9h9AT14_A.title: Ramadan 2023, Night 20: Quranic Reflections (Al-Ankabut to Al-Ahzab)
FI9h9AT14_A.one_line: Relationship surahs: debating with excellence, the rise and fall of nations, fitrah and simple faith, Luqman on arrogance, wake-up calls, and the Prophet at the Trench.
FI9h9AT14_A.summary: He continues the cluster on relationships, which he calls the secret of happiness, starting with Allah. Debate with the People of the Book only in the best way: start from shared revelation, behave and argue at your best, never make it about winning, since your own faith is a gift, and do not debate oppressors; remove oppression first. The Roman defeat in al-Rum teaches a universal law: everyone rises and falls, life is a zigzag, not a straight line, and our bodies follow the same arc, so humility is the right response. Setting your face to the deen means going all in on the fitrah, the innate sense of a Creator found in every civilization; Islam's appeal is its simplicity, and the rest follows from it. Luqman's warning against turning your cheek in arrogance shows that tazkiyah must start at home and early, so parents must learn it to pass it on before success breeds vanity in ambitious children. When our relationship with Allah goes stale, He sends lesser punishments as wake-up calls out of love; he urges people to return before they need one. The Prophet as the best example was revealed at the Trench, when believers' iman grew as things got darker.

outline.heading: Relationships as the secret of happiness
outline.gist: Research ties happiness to good relationships; Muslims agree and put the relationship with Allah first, and the cluster moves from people to life, Allah's laws, generations and Allah.

outline.heading: The next cluster: what submission really means
outline.gist: From al-Ahzab the surahs unpack obedience to Allah, which needs a whole group of surahs because it is not as simple as it sounds.

outline.heading: Interlude
Argue with the People of the Book only in the best way
outline.gist: Discussing faith with other communities demands your best words, ideas, intentions and behaviour.

outline.heading: Debates that become shouting matches
outline.gist: Public debates he watched as a boy taught crowds to jeer and mock, not to understand.

outline.heading: Except those who oppress: remove oppression first
outline.gist: You do not debate faith with an oppressor; Musa's first demand of Pharaoh was to free the enslaved, not to believe.

outline.heading: Begin with common ground
outline.gist: Say we believe in what was revealed to you and to us and our God is one; Islam does not erase others' faith or culture, it continues earlier revelation.

outline.heading: Engage only if you can do it with excellence
outline.gist: If you cannot bring your best ideas, articulation and conduct, stay out of these discussions.

outline.heading: Faith is a gift, not a contest
outline.gist: We are Muslim only because Allah blessed us, so acting as the winner who earned it is unacceptable.

outline.heading: The Romans defeated in the nearest land
outline.gist: Al-Rum opens on a documented war between the Persian and Byzantine empires east of present-day Syria.

outline.heading: They will win within a few years
outline.gist: The defeated would triumph within a few years, the matter is Allah's before and after, and the believers would rejoice.

outline.heading: Why the Muslims grieved for the Romans
outline.gist: The Romans held a revealed law while the Persians were fire-worshippers; Muslims see themselves as part of the human family and care who wins.

outline.heading: The law that days rotate among people
outline.gist: Victory and defeat change hands as a law of the universe that no willpower alters.

outline.heading: Abu Bakr's wager and the believers' own victory
outline.gist: Abu Bakr bet Quraysh the Romans would win within nine years, before betting was forbidden; another reading ties the joy to the Muslims' own victory at Badr.

outline.heading: Allah takes us out of the picture to teach a law
outline.gist: By describing a war between two non-Muslim powers, the Quran shows the rise-and-fall law applies to everyone.

outline.heading: Life is a zigzag, not a straight line
outline.gist: A trend line can rise, but the real data points always go up and down, and that is how life works.

outline.heading: Weakness, strength, then weakness again
outline.gist: Everything that goes up comes down; we peak and then even basic bodily functions fail, so we must meet this law with humility.

outline.heading: Set your face to the deen
outline.gist: The face stands for the whole self; Allah asks you to be all in for the deen.

outline.heading: Establish yourself as you establish prayer
outline.gist: As with establishing prayer, it means structure and readiness: bring your best in pure monotheism.

outline.heading: The fitrah: innate knowledge of a Creator
outline.gist: Every person carries the awareness of a power that made and watches over him; it gets buried under clutter but stays.

outline.heading: Every civilization built temples
outline.gist: Archaeologists find temples where schools are missing, because the human search for and struggle with God has always been there.

outline.heading: Speaking to the fitrah
outline.gist: When we speak about Allah we address what He placed in people; nothing changes His creation, though most choose not to see it.

outline.heading: Islam's appeal is its simplicity
outline.gist: Devote yourself to Allah in pure monotheism and believe in Him; that is the true religion.

outline.heading: Everything else follows from the root
outline.gist: Behaviours, rules and laws are consequences of that basic commitment; we overcomplicate by missing the root.

outline.heading: Luqman: a surah named after a wise man
outline.gist: The surah on generations carries the name of a man who was not a prophet, honoured for his wisdom.

outline.heading: Do not turn your cheek away in arrogance
outline.gist: Luqman warns his son against the twisted neck of the proud, likened to a camel disease, and walking the earth in vanity.

outline.heading: The building bricks of tazkiyah
outline.gist: Allah does not love the arrogant, and this awareness is the foundation of self-purification and self-accountability.

outline.heading: Tazkiyah starts at home
outline.gist: Parents must teach children to understand their inner drives, fears, greed, jealousy and arrogance, and that the nafs pulls toward selfishness.

outline.heading: You cannot give what you do not have
outline.gist: If parents lack this understanding they cannot pass it on, and no imam can sit with every child.

outline.heading: The monster on the inside
outline.gist: Prophets were sent to purify; the evil within outranks anything outside, so it must be faced young.

outline.heading: No one is born humble
outline.gist: Humility takes effort; without it the nafs turns vain after a little skill or success.

outline.heading: Successful children need checks on vanity
outline.gist: We want our youth powerful and capable, but unaddressed arrogance will corrupt their work in masjid, politics or business.

outline.heading: Every relationship can grow stale, even with Allah
outline.gist: Spouses, siblings and friends lose their spark, and young people after a sincere repentance often plateau in their faith.

outline.heading: Sides that forsake their beds
outline.gist: True believers fall into prostration when reminded and cannot stay in bed because they miss standing before Allah.

outline.heading: A taste of the lesser punishment
outline.gist: For those who drift, Allah sends a lesser punishment in this life so they might return and avoid the greater one.

outline.heading: Every slap from life is a reminder
outline.gist: Loss, fear, missed goals and a lost position are tastes of the lesser punishment meant to turn us back.

outline.heading: A log on the path, not a cliff
outline.gist: A fall from your bicycle is better than riding the wrong way until you go off a cliff.

outline.heading: Anyone over forty knows
outline.gist: Everyone eventually takes a hard fall after the relationship goes cold; the wise use it to return to Allah.

outline.heading: He sends it because He loves you
outline.gist: The wake-up call comes because Allah wants you back and you have stopped seeing what He already gave you.

outline.heading: Wake up before the wake-up call
outline.gist: Worship while things go well; waiting for something painful to return is the path most take, but it is needless.

outline.heading: The Trench: the hardest days of the sahaba
outline.gist: Ten thousand warriors camped outside Madinah for weeks amid hunger, fear and betrayal.

outline.heading: Your role model, revealed at the hardest moment
outline.gist: Allah named the Prophet the best example when he lacked sleep, food and safety; look at him then and follow him.

outline.heading: This is what Allah and His Messenger promised
outline.gist: Seeing the confederates, the believers only grew in faith and submission.

outline.heading: The darker it gets, the stronger the iman
outline.gist: The sign of a true movement is faith rising as things get harder; that is how to follow the Prophet.

outline.heading: Outro

themes.label: Allah's laws in history and the universe (sunan)
themes.note: Nations and people rise and fall in turn; life is a zigzag, which calls for humility.

themes.label: Tawhid and worship of Allah alone
themes.note: The fitrah holds an innate knowledge of the Creator; pure monotheism is simple and everything else follows from it.

themes.label: Humility vs vanity and arrogance
themes.note: Luqman's warning against arrogance; no one is born humble and success breeds vanity unless checked.

themes.label: Parenting and raising children
themes.note: Tazkiyah has to be taught at home and early, so parents must learn it themselves.

themes.label: Spirituality, khushoo and the inner life
themes.note: The relationship with Allah can plateau like any other; true believers long to rise and pray.

themes.label: Trials, hardship and resilience
themes.note: Hardships are lesser punishments sent out of love to bring us back; return before you need one.
